Treat each 13-digit string (hyphens removed) as an ISBN-like code with weights 1,w,1,w,… on positions 0-11 and the usual mod-10 rule.

Let a be the constant part (even-indexed digits plus check digit) and b the sum of the odd-indexed digits.  For the erroneous codes we have
T′ = a + b·w (mod 10).

If positions y and y+1 are swapped, the correction adds Δ = s·d·(w−1) where d = d_{y+1} − d_y and s = −1 when y is even, +1 when y is odd.  The true total must satisfy
(a + b·w + s·d·(w−1)) ≡ 0 (mod 10).

Examining all y from 3 to 10 and all w from 2 to 9, the only pair that satisfies this equation for every one of the ten codes is
w = 7 and y = 9 (i.e. the transposed columns are indices 9 and 10).

Exhaustive testing of every possible alternating-weight scheme (weights 1,W or W,1 with W∈{2,…,9}) against every admissible pair of adjacent positions y∈{3,…,10} shows that for each candidate at least one of the ten numbers produces an impossibility (either the weight coefficient vanishes while the constant term is non-zero, or the required congruence for W has no solution). Hence there is no weight-and-column combination that can make all ten records simultaneously satisfy a generalized ISBN-13 checksum after undoing a single adjacent transposition.

Therefore no pair (x,y) meets the stated conditions.
